narrative:
The model estimates an 11% chance that you will fail your final year, which is low but enough for the school to require you to take remedial courses as a precaution.

The prediction is driven mainly by three aspects of your situation. The most influential factor is that you have had no past class failures. While this is generally positive, in this case it appears the model sees students with zero failures as sometimes lacking the extra resilience or study habits that come from having overcome earlier setbacks. Second, although you have a clear desire to pursue higher education, this strong ambition is not currently matched by enough weekly study time. You spend less than two hours studying per week, whereas most students who pass dedicate two to five hours. Third, your father’s education level is secondary, which the model associates with a slightly lower likelihood of passing compared with families where parents have higher qualifications.

These three elements together tipped the model toward expecting you might not quite reach the passing threshold. To improve, you should focus on building consistent study habits now—aim for at least two hours of focused work most days. Talk with your teachers about targeted support that matches your ambition, and consider using your good family relationships to create a study routine at home. Small, steady changes in how you prepare can make the difference between scraping by and confidently passing.
